Example
We display a few specific artists from the Billboard Songs database and the top positions of their songs.

specific_artists <- df |>
  filter(artist %in% c("Ed Sheeran", "Adele", "Taylor Swift")) |>
  distinct(song, artist, peak.rank)

sd <- SharedData$new(specific_artists, key = ~song)

filter_checkbox("artist_checkbox", "Artist", sd, ~artist)

title: Exercise 7
text:
Problem 1

df <- data.frame(
x = c(5, 1, 4, NA, NA, NA, 2, 1),
y = c(5, NA, 3, 2, 5, NA, 2, 1),
z = c(1, 4, 2, 5, 2, NA, 5, 4),
t = c(4, 2, NA, 1, 5, 2, 3, 3)
)

r_yx <- cor(df$y, df$x, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
r_yz <- cor(df$y, df$z, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
r_yt <- cor(df$y, df$t, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

r_yx

[1] 0.9621405

r_yz

[1] -0.8327178

r_yt

[1] 0.72075


I will only be using User 4 since there is a positive correlation between User 4 and User 2, and User 4 is the only user with a rating for movie 6.

y_movie6_pref <- (r_yt/r_yt) * (2 - mean(df$t, na.rm = TRUE)) + mean(df$y, na.rm = TRUE)
y_movie6_pref

[1] 2.142857




Problem 2

movies <- as.data.frame(t(df))

for (i in 2:ncol(movies)) {
  correlation <- cor(
    as.numeric(movies[, 1]),
    as.numeric(movies[, i]),
    use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
  )
  
  print(paste("Movie", i, ":", correlation))
}

[1] "Movie 2 : -0.995870594885822"
[1] "Movie 3 : 0.866025403784439"
[1] "Movie 4 : -0.884615384615385"
[1] "Movie 5 : 0.970725343394151"
[1] "Movie 6 : NA"
[1] "Movie 7 : -0.996116490183505"
[1] "Movie 8 : -0.909799269869811"


The movie most similar to Movie 1 is Movie 5 since it has the highest Pearson correlation value when comparing all movies.


Problem 3A

countries <- read.csv("https://manctsui.github.io/datasets/countries.csv")

reactable(countries, searchable = TRUE, defaultPageSize = 5)




countries_clean <- countries |>
  group_by(Region) |>
  mutate(
    Agriculture = ifelse(is.na(Agriculture), mean(Agriculture, na.rm = TRUE), Agriculture),
    Industry = ifelse(is.na(Industry), mean(Industry, na.rm = TRUE), Industry)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

reactable(countries_clean, searchable = TRUE, defaultPageSize = 5)







Problem 3B

print(paste("Count of NAs in Agriculture: ", sum(is.na(countries$Agriculture))))

[1] "Count of NAs in Agriculture:  15"

print(paste("Count of NAs in Industry: ", sum(is.na(countries$Industry))))

[1] "Count of NAs in Industry:  16"




Problem 4

df <- data.frame(
temp = c(79, 74, 73, 76, 82, 72, 71, 79, 83, 70, 73, 75, 77),
chirps = c(44, 40, 38, 43, 48, 37, 34, 45, 51, 32, 35, 42, 43)
)

lm(temp ~ chirps, data = df)


Call:
lm(formula = temp ~ chirps, data = df)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)       chirps  
     46.474        0.714  

print(paste("Correlation: ", cor(df$temp, df$chirps)))

[1] "Correlation:  0.970876029231998"

print(paste("Mean temp: ", mean(df$temp)))

[1] "Mean temp:  75.6923076923077"

print(paste("Standard deviation temp: ", sd(df$temp)))

[1] "Standard deviation temp:  4.11064908468674"

print(paste("Mean chirps: ", mean(df$chirps)))

[1] "Mean chirps:  40.9230769230769"

print(paste("Standard deviation chirps: ", sd(df$chirps)))

[1] "Standard deviation chirps:  5.58959656358039"


The slope of a linear regression can be calculated using the correlation and standard deviations:
\[
b_1 = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}
\]
Using the values calculated from the data:
\[
b_1 = (0.970876)\left(\frac{4.110649}{5.589597}\right)
\]
\[
b_1 \approx 0.714
\]
Next, the intercept can be calculated using the means:
\[
b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}
\]
Substituting the values for temperature and chirps:
\[
b_0 = 75.692308 - (0.714)(40.923077)
\]
\[
b_0 \approx 46.474
\]
Therefore, the regression equation is:
\[
\widehat{temp} = 46.474 + 0.714(chirps)
\]
This is the same line of best fit produced by lm(temp ~ chirps, data = df). Therefore, the correlation, means, and standard deviations contain the information needed to calculate the slope and intercept of the linear regression line.

Problem 3 & 4

Code
UCLA_rankings$world_rank <- as.numeric(UCLA_rankings$world_rank)

ggplot(UCLA_rankings, aes(x = year, y = world_rank)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "UCLA World Rank by Year", x = "Year", y = "World Rank") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(7, 16)) +
  scale_y_reverse()
UCBERK_rankings <- data |>
  filter(grepl("Berkeley", university_name)) |>
  arrange(year)

UCBERK_rankings$world_rank <- as.numeric(UCBERK_rankings$world_rank)

ggplot(UCBERK_rankings, aes(x = year, y = world_rank)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "UC Berkeley World Rank by Year", x = "Year", y = "World Rank") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(7, 16)) +
  scale_y_reverse()



















Figure 1





Problem 5


Code
top_50_universities <- data |>
  filter(world_rank <= 50)

count_us_top_universities_year <- top_50_universities |>
  group_by(country, year) |>
  summarise(num_top_universities = n_distinct(university_name), .groups = "drop") |>

title: Exercise 6
text:
data <- read.csv("https://manctsui.github.io/datasets/timesData.csv")
reactable(data, searchable = T, defaultPageSize = 5)






Problem 1A

num_universities_by_country <- data |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(num_universities = n_distinct(university_name)) |>
  arrange(desc(num_universities)) |>
  head(3)

reactable(num_universities_by_country)







Problem 1B

ggplot(num_universities_by_country, aes(x=country, y=num_universities)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")










Problem 2A

top_50_unis_2011 <- data |>
  filter(year == 2011, as.numeric(world_rank) <= 50) |>
  select(world_rank, university_name) |>
  arrange(as.numeric(world_rank))

reactable(top_50_unis_2011, searchable = T, defaultPageSize = 5)







Problem 2B
When turning data into a SharedData object we want a key that is unique to each row of data. If this is talking about Problem 1A, using something like rank as a key is irrelevant, there is not regard to the ranking in the data set from problem 1A. However, if this is about problem 2A, then it is still not a great choice. world_rank has the possibility of being shared between two universities even in the same year, for example both the University of California, Irvine, and University of Science and Technology of China both share the world_rank of 49. There are 4 universities that share the world_rank of 43. world_rank does not function well as a unique identifier, but university_name would, and is a much better choice for the key.


Problem 2C

sd_top_50_2011 <- SharedData$new(top_50_unis_2011, key = ~university_name)

filter_slider("rank_slider", "Rank", sd_top_50_2011, column = ~as.numeric(world_rank))


Rank




reactable(sd_top_50_2011, searchable = T, defaultPageSize = 5)







Problem 3

data_2016 <- data |>
  filter(year == 2016) |>
  mutate(num_students = parse_number(num_students))

sd_2016 <- SharedData$new(data_2016, key = ~university_name)

plot_ly(
  sd_2016,
  x = ~student_staff_ratio,
  y = ~num_students,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Number of Students by Student Staff Ratio",
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Student Staff Ratio",
      nticks = 8
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Number of Students",
      tickformat = ",",
      nticks = 8
    )
  )




plot_ly(
  sd_2016,
  x = ~student_staff_ratio,
  y = ~teaching,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Teaching Score by Student Staff Ratio",
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Student Staff Ratio",
      nticks = 8
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Teaching Score",
      tickformat = ",",
      nticks = 8
    )
  )
